newsitem.title: THAILAND: FEATURE - Thailand's fortunes dive as problems dog economy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Thailand's fortunes dive as problems dog economy.

text.p: Thailand has seen its fortunes sour dramatically in less than a year, from being an envied booming Asian economic tiger to a nation gripped by a crisis of confidence.

Thailand's image has been buffeted since mid-1996 by waves of bad news -- zero export growth, big current account deficits two years in a row, surging foreign debt, market attacks on its once stable baht, and troubled financial institutions.
"The boom is over and we are riding on a bust that will take a few years to get out," said a foreign analyst at a brokerage firm who declined to be named.
Thailand's fast deteriorating position has produced the spectre of its sovereign long-term debt rating being downgraded by Moody's Investors Service that could aggravate its problems.
THAI RATING DOWNGRADE WOULD AGGRAVATE PROBLEMS

Moody's last month put Thailand's A2 credit rating on review for possible downgrade on concerns over a fast buildup of short-term foreign debt by private financial institutions, their exposure to a troubled property sector, and a steady rise in non-performing loans.
A sovereign debt downgrade would automatically hurt Moody's ratings of key Thai banks and cost them more to borrow abroad.
Of Thailand's $89.6 billion outstanding foreign debt at end-1996, 82 percent was tapped by the private sector and 43.7 percent was short-term borrowing.
Thailand's decision to lift foreign exchange controls in 1991 and its bid to attract foreign capital by keeping domestic interest rates high have driven corporate borrowers abroad in recent years.
Money market analysts estimated that Thai private companies borrowed about $9 billion in fresh foreign loans last year, half of which were underwritten by Singapore-based arrangers.
TROUBLED FINANCE FIRMS BRACE FOR MERGERS

Analysts said severe liquidity problems of the ailing 90-company finance sector because of high interest rates, would force the industry to consolidate through mergers and acquisitions in the next one to two years

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan and central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond took steps this week to strengthen banks and finance firms by ordering them to raise provisions for doubtful loans and substandard assets.

Rerngchai also named 10 cash-strapped finance companies instructed by the central bank to raise capital by a combined 8.25 billion baht ($319.8 million) so as to assure their creditors that they could continue to operate soundly.

The spark that ignited public runs on deposits at finance companies this week was a March 1 agreement on a friendly merger between Finance One Plc, Thailand's biggest finance company, and Thai Danu Bank Plc.
The merger announcement came after weeks of rumours that Finance One faced short-term liquidity problems.
THAILAND SHOULD LEARN FROM CRISIS NOT PANIC
Economist Somjai Phagaphasvivat of Thammasat University, however, cautioned against panic, saying Thailand should try to learn a lesson from its problems.

He said: "We are looking at a crisis but the problems are not insurmountable. With cooperation from all sides, we still could move ahead. We should strive to turn this crisis into a blessing in disguise but we must not let complacency set in."

Others saw the latest government action as an attempt to impress Moody's that Thailand would move to beef up its finance sector. Nearly 100 billion baht in spending cuts announced last month were aimed at narrowing a wide current account deficit.
Rerngchai said on Wednesday the higher provisions should be put in place before financial institutions are required to detail non-performing loans in their quarterly balance sheets from mid-1997.
He said increased reserves for low quality assets would make their financial statements look more respectable.
FINANCE SECTOR HURT BY LOANS TO PROPERTY DEVELOPERS

The economic downturn has been accompanied by a four-year slump of the property sector and a precipitous decline of the Thai stock market where the SET composite index has retreated 48.7 percent in the past 12 months.
The index closed on Thursday at 676.65, its lowest level since May 19, 1992, when it finished at 667.84.
The mounting problems have shaken banks, finance and brokerage firms, especially those with big exposure to the property sector.
Most of Thailand's 41 listed finance and securities firms extended about a quarter of their loans to the troubled property sector and earned about 20 percent of their revenue from stock broking fees.

An analyst at Krungthai Thanakit Plc estimated that at least 8.8 percent of bank and finance company loans could be classified as doubtful or sub-standard and their poor asset quality would decline further in the next several months.
"Because of its last property boom (in the early 1990s), Thailand has a generation of investors who still could not conceive that land prices here can be written down," he said.
THAI EXPORTS LOSE COMPETITIVENESS
Somjai said Thailand's current plight could partly be attributed to failure of the previous government of Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa to acknowledge export problems in their early stage.

Analysts said Thailand could lose competitiveness for computers and printed circuit boards, its biggest exports, in a few years when Latin American countries join the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).
Thailand's export-driven economy expanded 6.7 percent in 1996, its slowest growth in a decade, and 8.7 percent in 1995.
Thai exports, growing in double digits annually during the first half of this decade, contracted 0.2 percent in 1996 against 23.6 percent increase in 1995.

"In mid-1996, we were shocked by eight percent export growth for the first half year but the government argued that the decline was cyclical. They did not take time to find out if we were losing competitiveness," Somjai said.
